chapter.title: Agent, chatbot, or plain script: picking the right tool

cards.body: Renaming 500 files needs no agent. Sorting 50 emails might. Think of the intern: you'd never hire someone smart and eager just to stamp 500 envelopes the same way. You'd buy a stamp, because **the intern is for work where every step needs a fresh decision.**
cards.simpler: Renaming 500 files doesn't need an agent. Sorting 50 emails might. Picture an intern. You wouldn't hire someone smart and keen just to stamp 500 envelopes the same way. You'd buy a rubber stamp instead. That's because **the intern is for work where every step needs a fresh decision.**

cards.prompt: You have 500 holiday photos with names like IMG_4031.jpg. You want them renamed Lisbon-001 to Lisbon-500, in the order they were taken. Who gets the job?

options.text: An agent, so it can think about each photo
A plain script: fixed steps the computer repeats exactly
A chatbot, so you can just ask

whyNot.a: That's the intern, not the stamp: nothing here needs a decision, so 500 rounds of thinking only add cost.
whyNot.c: That's answering, not doing: a chatbot tells you how, then stops, and you're still the one renaming.

cards.reteach: Could you write every step on a sticky note before you start? Here you could: next photo, next number, repeat. A path that fixed belongs to a script.

cards.title: Two questions about the path
cards.body:
The first question: **is the path known in advance?** If you could write every step on a sticky note before starting, you want a *script*, a fixed list of instructions the computer follows exactly. It's quick and cheap, and it never improvises.

The second question: does each step need judgement? If step 4 depends on what turned up at step 3, nobody can write that sticky note ahead of time. That's where the intern earns their desk.

And if all you need is an answer or a draft, and you'll do the acting yourself, a chatbot is enough.
cards.simpler:
First question: **is the path known in advance?** If you could write every step on a sticky note first, you want a script: a fixed list of steps the computer follows exactly. It's quick, cheap and never improvises.

Second question: does each step need judgement? If step 4 depends on what step 3 turned up, no sticky note works. That's the intern's job.

If you only need an answer or draft and will act yourself, a chatbot is enough.

cards.title: Maya's Monday inbox
cards.body: Maya opens her laptop on Monday to 50 new emails. A script can handle half of them: anything from a 'noreply' address goes into Newsletters, with the same rule every time. The other half need reading. Her landlord's 'quick thing' could be a rent rise or a broken boiler. Her mum's 'Garage SALE Saturday?' is not a promotion, whatever a keyword rule thinks. **That second pile is agent work: read, decide, file, next.**
cards.simpler: On Monday, Maya opens her laptop to 50 new emails. A script can deal with half of them. Anything from a 'noreply' address goes into Newsletters, with the same rule every time. The other half need reading. Her landlord's 'quick thing' could be a rent rise or a broken boiler. Her mum's 'Garage SALE Saturday?' isn't an advert, whatever a simple word-matching rule thinks. **That second pile is agent work: read, decide, file, next.**

cards.prompt: You want the best robot vacuum under £300. That means reading reviews, spotting paid ads and following links you can't predict. Which setup fits?

options.text: A script that checks the same 5 review sites
An agent that researches and hands you a shortlist; you press buy
A chatbot you ask once, then trust

whyNot.a: That's a known path, and this isn't one: which pages matter depends on what you read first.
whyNot.c: That's one answer, not many steps: a chatbot replies and stops.

cards.reteach: Research is a path you find as you walk it, so every step needs judgement: that's agent work. Keeping the buy button for yourself is the third question at work, because a wrong purchase costs real money.

cards.title: The third question: what does a mistake cost?
cards.body:
Even when an agent fits, ask **how bad is a wrong move?** A mislabelled email costs you three seconds to drag back. A £280 order or a message to your boss can't be unsent. The higher the cost, the shorter the leash: make it ask before acting, or keep that step for yourself.

You'd think the smartest tool is always the best pick. It's the reverse. The best tool is the simplest one that does the job. A script can't make anything up or wander off. Start there. Hire the intern only when the steps truly can't be written down.
cards.simpler:
Even with an agent, ask **how bad is a wrong move?** A misfiled email takes three seconds to fix. A £280 order or a note to your boss can't be unsent. The bigger the cost, the shorter the leash: make it ask first, or do it yourself.

The best tool is the simplest that does the job, not the smartest. A script can't make things up or wander off, so start there. Use the intern only when steps can't be written down.

cards.body: Sam asks an agent to rename 500 files to a simple pattern. Forty minutes and 500 model calls later, it's mostly done, except for file 312, which it decided deserved the name 'beach_sunset_best'. A 5-line script would have finished in two seconds with zero opinions. **If you can write the steps down before you start, it's a script, not an agent.**
cards.simpler: Sam asks an agent to rename 500 files using a simple pattern. Forty minutes and 500 calls to the AI later, it's mostly done. Except file 312, which it decided should be called 'beach_sunset_best'. A five-line script would have finished in two seconds, with no opinions at all. **If you can write the steps down before you start, it's a script, not an agent.**

cards.prompt: A friend says: 'Agents are the smartest option, so I'll use one for everything.' What's the best reply?

options.text: Fair, the smartest tool always does the best job
Only when each step needs judgement; known steps go to a script, which can't improvise
Only where mistakes are expensive, since agents are careful

whyNot.a: That's Sam's 500 files: thinking costs time and money, and it adds room to wander.
whyNot.c: That's the third question flipped: costly mistakes call for a shorter leash, not more agent.

cards.reteach: You don't put an intern on a job a stamp can do. Known steps go to a script, a single answer goes to a chatbot, and only a path you discover step by step goes to an agent.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Before you pick a tool, ask three things: is the path known, does each step need judgement, and what does a mistake cost? A known path means a script, one answer means a chatbot, and a path you find step by step means an agent, with a human yes before anything you can't undo.

Next: run a ready-made agent on your own computer and choose what it may touch.
cards.simpler:
Before you pick a tool, **ask three questions**. Is the path known? Does each step need judgement? What does a mistake cost? A known path means a script. A single answer means a chatbot. A path you find step by step means an agent, and a human says yes before anything that can't be undone.

Next, you'll run a ready-made agent on your own computer and choose what it's allowed to touch.

cards.body: Write down 3 tasks from your week, like paying bills or planning a trip. For each one, answer the three questions in one word apiece, then label it script, chatbot or agent.
cards.simpler: Write down three tasks from your week, like paying bills or planning a trip. For each one, answer the three questions with one word each: is the path known, does each step need judgement, and what does a mistake cost? Then **label each task script, chatbot or agent.**

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now run any task through 3 questions and say whether it needs an agent, a chatbot, or a plain script.
